If you’re investing time, money, and energy in events, you want to know they’re worth it. Leadership wants to know too, usually the week after the event ends. Measuring **event ROI** gives you a clear answer: what the event cost, what it returned, and which parts delivered the most value.


In this guide, we cover what event ROI means, the formula to calculate it, and the 7 metrics that show the full picture, from attendance to media coverage.

##


**What Is Event ROI?**


Event ROI (return on investment) compares what an event earned with what it cost. Teams usually count revenue, pipeline and qualified leads as the return, and venue, staff, marketing, and technology as the cost. A positive event ROI means the event created more value than it consumed, and a negative one means it cost more than it returned.


Event ROI matters because events are one of the biggest line items in most marketing budgets. A clear number helps you defend the budget, compare events, and decide where to invest next year.


##


**How Do You Calculate Event ROI?**


To calculate event ROI, subtract the total event cost from the revenue the event generated, divide by the total cost, and multiply by 100. For example, an event that cost $40,000 and generated $100,000 in closed revenue has an ROI of 150%. Use pipeline instead of revenue when deals take months to close.


**Event ROI (%)** = Event revenue − Total event cost


Total event cost


× 100


The hard part is not the math. The hard part is agreeing on what counts as revenue and cost and collecting the data in one place. Our free **[event ROI calculator](https://inevent.com/en/event-roi-calculator.php)** does the math for you once you have the numbers.


Our team spans 13+ countries, and our event strategists see the same pattern in every market: the events that prove their ROI are the ones that defined it before the doors opened.


***Team Tip:*** *Agree on the ROI definition with finance before the event, not after. Decide whether you count closed revenue, pipeline, or both, and set the attribution window (30, 60, or 90 days). Most ROI arguments happen because sales and marketing used different windows.*


##


**What Are the Most Important Event ROI Metrics?**


The most important event ROI metrics are attendance rate, engagement rate, lead generation, social media engagement, total event cost, customer satisfaction, and media coverage. Together, they show both the financial return and the softer value, like brand reach and loyalty. Track all seven in one place, so the numbers agree when you report them.


Metric Formula What it tells you


**Attendance rate** Attendees ÷ registrants × 100 How well promotion converted sign-ups


**Engagement rate** Interactions ÷ attendees How active guests were in sessions and the app


**Cost per lead** Total event cost ÷ qualified leads Lead efficiency vs other channels


**Pipeline** Value of open deals touched by the event Revenue still in progress


**Net Promoter Score** % promoters − % detractors Likelihood guests return or refer


### **1. Attendance Rate**


Attendance rate is the number of people who attended divided by the number who registered, multiplied by 100. A high attendance rate shows your promotion and reminder emails worked. A low one points to weak reminders, a poor date or a free ticket with no commitment.


Track attendance by session too, not just at the door. Our


**[attendee journey report](https://inevent.com/en/attendee-journey-historical-report.php)** shows where each guest went, so you can see which sessions pulled the crowd.


### **2. Engagement Rate**


Engagement rate measures how actively attendees took part during the event. Divide the total interactions (poll answers, questions asked, chat messages, meetings booked, and app actions) by the number of attendees. A rising engagement rate means your content and format are working.


Engaged attendees remember your brand, stay for more sessions, and are more likely to talk to sales. To increase it, try these


**[21 event engagement ideas](https://inevent.com/blog/events/20-event-engagement-ideas.html)** .


### **3. Lead Generation**


Events are one of the best ways to


**[generate leads](https://inevent.com/blog/marketing/lead-generation-for-online-events-7-tips-to-rock-your-event.html)** . Track the number of new qualified leads and your cost per lead, then compare it with other channels like paid ads or webinars.


Don’t stop at the lead count. Follow each lead into your CRM and report pipeline influenced (the value of open deals the event touched) and revenue closed within 90 days. Those two numbers are what leadership usually wants to see.


In our platform, every badge tap, booked meeting, and session scan lands in the attendee’s record and syncs to your CRM, so pipeline reporting can start the day the event ends instead of weeks later.


### **4. Social Media Engagement**


Social media engagement shows how far your event traveled beyond the room. Track likes, shares, comments, mentions and posts using your event hashtag before, during, and after the event. Compare the numbers with your last event to see whether your promotion is growing your reach.


### 5. Total Cost of the Event


Total event cost is the bottom half of the ROI formula, so you need to complete it. Include venue, catering, travel, staff time, speakers, marketing, technology, printing, and shipping. Missing costs make your ROI look better than it is, and finance will notice. Keep every cost in one budget from the start, not in separate spreadsheets. For in-person events, see our guide to[measuring the ROI of in-person events](https://inevent.com/blog/others/measuring-the-roi-of-in-person-events-what-metrics-to-consider.html)


### **6. Customer Satisfaction**


Customer satisfaction tells you whether guests valued the event and would come back. Send a short post-event survey within 24 hours, while the experience is fresh. Ask for an overall rating, a Net Promoter Score question and one open question about what to improve.


Keep it to five questions or fewer. Short surveys get more answers, and more answers give you numbers you can trust.


### **7. Media Coverage**


Media coverage measures the earned attention your event created. Track press mentions, articles, podcast features and partner posts, and note the reach of each outlet. Coverage in respected industry publications also builds the brand authority that AI search engines use when choosing sources to cite. Muck Rack’s latest[What Is AI Reading? study](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/10/28/3390134/0/en/generative-pulse-earned-media-still-drives-more-than-84-of-ai-citations.html) found that earned media drives more than 84% of the sources major AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini cite, while paid and advertorial content makes up just 0.3%.


Timing matters too. An[earlier Muck Rack report](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/03/30/3264743/0/en/New-Research-Finds-Earned-Media-Accounts-for-25-of-All-Large-Language-Model-Citations.html) found AI citation rates peak in the first seven days after publication. Pitch your event recap, speaker highlights, and key stats to industry media within a week of the event, while the story is still fresh for journalists and AI engines alike.


##


**Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What is a good ROI for an event?**


A good event ROI is any return above 0%, and revenue-focused events like trade shows or sales kickoffs should target higher. What counts as good depends on the event’s goal. A brand or customer event may show low direct revenue but strong retention, so set the ROI target before planning starts and judge results against it.


### **How do you measure ROI for a virtual or hybrid event?**


Virtual and hybrid event ROI uses the same formula as in-person events. The difference is the data: track online attendance minutes, session drop-off, chat and poll activity, and on-demand views. Because costs like venue and catering are lower, virtual events often show a higher ROI per attendee than in-person ones.


### **What is the difference between event ROI and ROO?**


Event ROI measures financial return, while return on objectives (ROO) measures whether the event met non-financial goals. ROO covers aims like brand awareness, attendee satisfaction, or partner relationships. Most teams report both: ROI for leadership and finance, and ROO for goals revenue alone doesn’t capture.


### **How soon after an event should you measure ROI?**


Measure event ROI twice: an early read within one week and a full read after 60 to 90 days. The early read covers attendance, engagement, and leads. The later read adds closed deals and pipeline, which in B2B often take months to land after the event.
